claims.description: An internet attacker can flood `process:web-server` through the boundary-crossing `flow:reader-to-web-server:page-requests`. Each request consumes HTTPS and CMS request-handling capacity; the CMS maintains pages, accounts, and comments in `store:mysql-database`, so request processing can also propagate load to the database. Request-rate limits, request-size/complexity bounds, caching behavior, worker limits, and load shedding are not stated in the model, so this threat is conditional on those unverified availability controls being insufficient. Second-order, saturation prevents legitimate readers from reaching the public site and can add load to `store:mysql-database`, impairing CMS reads and writes.

If the latter flow's `authentication: unknown` resolves to absent, weak, or otherwise attacker-obtainable access controls, an attacker from `boundary:public-internet` can open and hold MySQL connections or issue resource-intensive maintenance queries against the store. Second-order, `process:web-server` loses the data store it uses for pages, accounts, and comments, so legitimate site requests and CMS writes fail alongside direct administration.

mitigations.detail: Encrypt `store:mysql-database` and all backups and snapshots with managed keys, and record the confirmed `encryption_at_rest` control in the model.

mitigations.summary: Validate database restores before use
mitigations.detail: Use signed or checksummed backups, controlled restore identities, and integrity verification before restored MySQL data is accepted by `process:web-server`.

claims.title: Plaintext CDN delivery lets an on-path attacker impersonate the CDN to readers
claims.description: An attacker able to intercept public-network traffic can substitute a look-alike `entity:cdn` for `entity:reader` on `flow:reader-to-cdn:asset-fetch`, because the boundary-crossing asset fetch uses HTTP with encryption in transit stated absent. The attacker can present attacker-controlled images, stylesheets, or downloads as CDN content. The derived crossing places `entity:cdn` in `boundary:cdn` using an inferred endpoint placement; regardless, the reader-facing flow originates on `boundary:public-internet` and lacks transport server authenticity. Second-order: readers consume the substituted public-site assets, creating a public content-authenticity and reputation risk.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because `flow:reader-to-cdn:asset-fetch` crosses from `boundary:public-internet` and has encryption in transit stated absent, but exploitation requires an on-path or traffic-redirection position. Impact is low because the stated payload is public images, stylesheets, and downloads; the model does not establish that this flow carries credentials, PII, or privileged actions.

mitigations.summary: Require authenticated HTTPS for all CDN asset delivery
mitigations.detail: Configure `flow:reader-to-cdn:asset-fetch` for TLS 1.2+ with valid certificate-chain validation and redirect or reject HTTP, so readers can authenticate `entity:cdn` before accepting assets.

mitigations.summary: Constrain CDN certificate issuance
mitigations.detail: Use an appropriate certificate-management policy, such as CAA and tightly controlled CDN certificate issuance, to reduce the chance that a substituted endpoint can obtain a trusted certificate.

claims.title: Unauthorized asset publication is possible if CDN upload authentication is absent
claims.description: `flow:web-server-to-cdn-bucket:asset-publish` crosses from `boundary:hosted-network` to `boundary:cdn`, but its `authentication` attribute is unknown. If that unknown resolves to no verified caller identity, an attacker able to reach the upload endpoint can impersonate `process:web-server` to `store:cdn-bucket` and publish assets as though they came from the CMS. Second-order: `entity:reader` subsequently fetches those published images, stylesheets, and downloads through the CDN, so the spoofed service identity becomes a distribution path for attacker-controlled public content. This draft is conditional on the unknown authentication state; it does not assert that upload authentication is absent.

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `authentication` on `flow:web-server-to-cdn-bucket:asset-publish`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is low and conditional on the unknown authentication value: an attacker must first obtain reachability to the CDN upload interface from outside `boundary:hosted-network`, and a verification control may exist but be undocumented. Impact is medium because successful impersonation writes attacker-selected published assets to `store:cdn-bucket`, which is tagged `business-critical-data`, for delivery to public readers.

mitigations.summary: Establish and enforce a unique workload identity for CDN publishing
mitigations.detail: Document `flow:web-server-to-cdn-bucket:asset-publish` authentication and require `process:web-server` to use a dedicated, short-lived workload identity or mutually authenticated TLS credential accepted only for its bucket-write role.

mitigations.summary: Require authenticated and encrypted CDN upload transport
mitigations.detail: Set the upload protocol and `encryption_in_transit` explicitly, require TLS with certificate validation, and restrict the bucket policy so only the verified `process:web-server` identity can publish.

claims.title: On-path attacker can alter static assets delivered to readers
claims.description: An attacker positioned between `entity:reader` and `entity:cdn` can modify HTTP responses on `flow:reader-to-cdn:asset-fetch`, replacing images, stylesheets, or downloads before they reach readers. Because this public-to-CDN flow has no transport integrity protection, readers receive attacker-controlled site assets as though supplied by the CDN. The alteration can affect the public site's presentation and downloaded content for every reader routed through the attacker.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because `flow:reader-to-cdn:asset-fetch` crosses from `boundary:public-internet` and explicitly lacks transport encryption, but exploitation requires an on-path or traffic-redirection position; impact is low because the model identifies only public images, stylesheets, and downloads, without establishing sensitive data or privileged actions.

mitigations.summary: Serve CDN assets over authenticated HTTPS
mitigations.detail: Require TLS with certificate validation on `flow:reader-to-cdn:asset-fetch` and redirect or block HTTP so an on-path party cannot replace responses.

mitigations.summary: Add integrity verification for executable downloads
mitigations.detail: Publish signed downloads and have clients verify signatures, so a modified artifact is rejected even if a delivery path is compromised.
